Executive Summary

What we already know

Hospital Background

Royal Liverpool University Hospital

Large acute hospital. Mainly focuses on complex planned care and specialist services. These include nephrology, renal transplantation, nuclear medicine, haematology, lithotripsy, dermatology and urology [@ref]. Provider also manage Aintree University hospital and Broadgreen hospital. Moved to new site single bed accommodation in October 2022. Prior to the change, the site had been operating 16.6% single bed room accommodation [@ERIC].

Clatterbridge Cancer Centre

Royal Papworth

Royal Papwroth hospital is a specialist centre for cardiothoracic (heart and lung) treatment, surgery and transplantation [@ref]. The move to single bed accommodation occured in May 2019. Prior to the change, the site had been operating 32.8% single bed room accommodation [@ERIC].

Clatterbridge (REN)

[1] "\n\nDuring the post-intervention period, the response variable had an average value of approx. 93.87. By contrast, in the absence of an intervention, we would have expected an average response of 97.61. The 95% interval of this counterfactual prediction is [94.99, 100.24]. Subtracting this prediction from the observed response yields an estimate of the causal effect the intervention had on the response variable. This effect is -3.74 with a 95% interval of [-6.37, -1.12]. For a discussion of the significance of this effect, see below.\n\nSumming up the individual data points during the post-intervention period (which can only sometimes be meaningfully interpreted), the response variable had an overall value of 1.03K. By contrast, had the intervention not taken place, we would have expected a sum of 1.07K. The 95% interval of this prediction is [1.04K, 1.10K].\n\nThe above results are given in terms of absolute numbers. In relative terms, the response variable showed a decrease of -4%. The 95% interval of this percentage is [-6%, -1%].\n\nThis means that the negative effect observed during the intervention period is statistically significant. If the experimenter had expected a positive effect, it is recommended to double-check whether anomalies in the control variables may have caused an overly optimistic expectation of what should have happened in the response variable in the absence of the intervention.\n\nThe probability of obtaining this effect by chance is very small (Bayesian one-sided tail-area probability p = 0.006). This means the causal effect can be considered statistically significant."

↑ indicates a significant increase post-switch to single rooms, while ↓ indicates a significant decrease.
Where a result is considered positive, e.g. decreased length of stay or increased patient experience score, it is coloured green, while a negative result is shown in red.
'-' indicates a non-significant change, which is shown in yellow.
Grey shading indicates where there was insufficient data to analyse.

Notes: For Royal Liverpool there is only 1 year post switch to single bedrooms, it is possible the effect size or overall direction of the effect may be different if there was a slightly longer outcome period. For some sites the outcome period is impacted by COVID-19, while COVID-19 effects are also present in the matched control sites, the magnitude of effects varies between hospitals/areas. There are also some situations where there is missing data or anomalies in the outcome periods, i.e. sudden jumps, which has meant the outcome period has been cut short.

Staff survey and cleaning costs data are an annual measure so there is limited data with only 2 data points in the outcome period.

Staff survey the data is collected over a period of time in the autumn each year, but for analysis purposes we have set the date as the last day of the year in which the data was collected. Both Chase Farm and Royal Liverpool switched to single rooms during the autumn, so the data for the first data point in the outcome period would actually have been collected during the transition period which may have had an impact on the results.
